headings.title: Introduction to Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) and Medicalisation
headings.content: Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) encompasses all procedures that involve partial or total removal of the external female genitalia or other injury to the female genital organs for non-medical reasons. Traditionally performed by traditional practitioners under unhygienic conditions, a dangerous trend known as the medicalisation of FGM has emerged. Medicalisation refers to situations where FGM is practiced by health care providers, such as doctors, nurses, midwives, or trained birth attendants, whether in public or private health facilities. The rationale often deceptively cited by practitioners includes minimizing pain, reducing infection risks, or using sterile instruments. However, medicalisation does not eliminate the severe health risks and lifelong complications associated with the procedure. More importantly, it legitimizes a harmful practice and violates fundamental human rights and medical ethics. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding this concept is vital, as it highlights how the misuse of clinical skills can compromise patient well-being and perpetuate gender-based violence under the guise of healthcare.

headings.title: Drivers and Sociocultural Contexts of Medicalised FGM
headings.content: The persistence of the medicalisation of FGM is driven by complex sociocultural contexts and pressures. In many communities where FGM is practiced, it is deeply embedded as a cultural norm, a rite of passage into womanhood, a marker of identity, and a prerequisite for marriage. Families may seek out health professionals to perform the procedure out of a misguided belief that 'safe' or clinical FGM avoids the severe, life-threatening complications associated with traditional methods. Furthermore, healthcare workers themselves are not immune to cultural conditioning; some may participate due to community pressure, fear of ostracisation, or financial gain. Economic incentives can be a powerful driver in under-resourced settings where providers supplement their income through the procedure. Additionally, misconceptions about religious mandates or hygiene preservation continue to fuel the demand for medicalised FGM. For nurses practicing in Nigeria, recognizing these socio-cultural and economic drivers is essential for designing effective, culturally sensitive community interventions that challenge the root causes of the practice rather than just addressing its clinical manifestations.

headings.title: Ethical and Legal Frameworks Against FGM Medicalisation
headings.content: The medicalisation of FGM is a direct violation of established ethical and legal frameworks. From an ethical standpoint, healthcare providers are bound by the core principles of biomedical ethics: beneficence (acting in the patient's best interest), non-maleficence (do no harm), autonomy, and justice. Performing FGM actively causes harm and violates non-maleficence, while also breaching the patient's autonomy, especially when performed on minors who cannot give informed consent. Internationally, treaties such as the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) and the Maputo Protocol explicitly condemn FGM. Regionally and nationally, Nigeria has enacted strong legislation, notably the Violence Against Persons Prohibition (VAPP) Act of 2015, which criminalizes all forms of FGM, including medicalisation. Professional regulatory bodies, such as the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN), view medicalisation as professional misconduct punishable by the revocation of licenses. Nursing students must understand that no cultural or religious justification overrides these legal and ethical prohibitions against practicing or facilitating FGM.

headings.title: Global and National Stances of Health Authorities
headings.content: Major global and national health authorities maintain a unified stance against the medicalisation of Female Genital Mutilation. Organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), and UNICEF, alongside international medical and nursing associations, have issued clear joint statements declaring that healthcare providers must never perform FGM under any circumstances. These bodies emphasize that medicalisation does not make the practice safe, nor does it reduce psychological trauma; rather, it legitimizes a human rights violation and falsely medicalises a non-medical procedure. In Nigeria, the Federal Ministry of Health, in collaboration with professional bodies like the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria and the Nigerian Medical Association, actively denounces the practice. Institutional policies mandate zero tolerance for any healthcare facility or professional engaging in FGM. Public health campaigns and regulatory oversight are continuously strengthened to detect and prosecute health workers who compromise professional integrity by performing or abetting FGM, reinforcing the message that clinical settings must remain sanctuaries of healing and rights protection.

headings.title: Physical, Psychological, and Reproductive Health Complications
headings.content: Regardless of whether FGM is performed by a traditional circumciser or a trained healthcare provider, the physical, psychological, and reproductive health complications are severe and often lifelong. Immediate physical complications include severe pain, excessive hemorrhage, shock, acute urinary retention, and localized infections such as tetanus and sepsis. Long-term physical consequences involve chronic pelvic pain, recurrent urinary tract infections, keloid formation, dyspareunia (painful sexual intercourse), and damage to adjacent urethral and vaginal structures. Reproductive health complications are particularly devastating, including obstructed labor, perineal tearing, obstetric fistulae, increased risk of caesarean sections, and higher rates of maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. Psychologically, survivors frequently suffer from anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), chronic fear, and deep-seated sexual dysfunction or loss of libido. Medicalised FGM provides a false sense of security regarding hygiene, but it cannot prevent these profound anatomical, physiological, and psychological traumas, making comprehensive care crucial for affected individuals.

headings.title: The Role of the Nurse in Prevention and Advocacy
headings.content: Nurses occupy a frontline position in the prevention of FGM and the elimination of its medicalisation. As educators, advocates, and care providers, nurses are uniquely positioned to influence community attitudes and protect vulnerable individuals. Prevention begins with community sensitization and health education, where nurses engage women, men, religious leaders, and youth groups to debunk myths surrounding FGM, highlight its severe health consequences, and emphasize its illegality under Nigerian law. In clinical practice, nurses must remain vigilant in identifying girls at risk during routine pediatric, immunization, or antenatal visits by conducting gentle, respectful risk assessments. Furthermore, nurses have a professional and ethical duty to report colleagues or other healthcare providers suspected of engaging in medicalised FGM to appropriate regulatory authorities. By participating in multidisciplinary advocacy campaigns, collaborating with non-governmental organizations, and upholding the highest standards of professional ethics, nurses act as powerful change agents dedicated to eradicating gender-based violence and safeguarding the health of women and girls.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Support for Survivors
headings.content: Providing nursing care and support for survivors of FGM requires a compassionate, holistic, and trauma-informed approach. Survivors may present in various healthcare settings—ranging from routine gynecological exams to labor and delivery—often carrying physical pain and emotional trauma. Nurses must establish a trusting, non-judgmental environment, ensuring patient privacy and informed consent during all physical examinations, as pelvic exams can trigger flashbacks of the trauma. Clinical management involves treating immediate complications like infections or hemorrhage, as well as managing long-term issues such as chronic pain, urinary problems, and sexual dysfunction. During obstetric care, nurses must be skilled in identifying complications early, providing sensitive intrapartum care, and advocating for necessary interventions like deinfibulation when appropriate. Furthermore, holistic care necessitates psychological support, active listening, and seamless referral to mental health counselors, social workers, or support groups specializing in trauma recovery. By addressing both the physical wounds and psychological scars, nurses play a transformative role in healing and empowering FGM survivors.
